passage: Many people think of deserts as places of constant heat. However, many deserts become surprisingly cold at night. Because dry desert air holds little moisture, the heat absorbed by the ground during the day escapes quickly after sunset, and temperatures can drop by more than 20 degrees Celsius.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain why deserts can become cold at night despite a common belief that they are always hot
To compare the climates of several different deserts
To argue that deserts are more dangerous to travelers than most people realize
To describe the plants and animals that survive in deserts
explanation:
For purpose questions, ask: why did the writer write this? Tracing what each sentence does helps.

Sentence 1 states a common belief: deserts are always hot. Sentence 2 pushes back with "However": they get cold at night. Sentence 3 explains why: dry air lets the day's heat escape.

So the purpose is to explain why deserts get cold at night, despite what people assume. That's choice A.

rationales.B: The text talks about deserts in general. It never compares particular deserts.
rationales.C: Danger to travelers never comes up. The text explains a temperature pattern.
rationales.D: No plants or animals are mentioned.

passage: In the 1920s, a small group of painters in one European city began creating works that rejected realistic detail in favor of bold colors and simple shapes. At first, critics mocked the paintings as childish and predicted the style would soon be forgotten. Within two decades, however, the same style was being taught in art schools across the continent.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a criticism of a painting style and then explains why the critics were correct.
It compares two painting styles and explains why one became more popular.
It describes how art schools trained painters and then explains why critics disliked their work.
It describes a new artistic style, presents an early negative reaction to it, and then notes its later widespread acceptance.
explanation:
For structure questions, label each sentence's job in a few words, then find the choice that lists those jobs in order.

Sentence 1: a new style appears. Sentence 2: critics mock it. Sentence 3, with "however": it ends up taught everywhere.

New style, early rejection, later acceptance. That's choice D.

rationales.A: The last sentence proves the critics wrong, not right. The style wasn't forgotten.
rationales.B: Only one style is described. It's set against realistic detail, not against a second named style.
rationales.C: This jumbles the order. Art schools only appear at the end, as proof the style caught on.

passage: Octopuses can change the color of their skin in a fraction of a second. They do this using thousands of tiny pigment sacs, which expand or shrink when the muscles around them contract or relax. For example, when an octopus rests against a patch of reddish coral, it can quickly give its skin a similar reddish tone. This ability helps octopuses hide from predators.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?
choices: It introduces a claim that the rest of the text disputes.
It explains how muscles control the pigment sacs in an octopus's skin.
It provides a specific example of the color-changing ability described earlier in the text.
It states the main conclusion that the rest of the text supports.
explanation:
Signal words often reveal a sentence's job. The third sentence starts with "For example," so it's giving a specific case of something said earlier.

The example is an octopus turning reddish to match coral, which is a concrete case of the color changing ability from the first sentence. That's choice C.

rationales.A: Nothing in the text argues against the third sentence. All the sentences support each other.
rationales.B: That's what the second sentence does. The third gives an example.
rationales.D: The main point comes in the first sentence. The third one supports it with an example.

passage:
The following text is from a story.

Ana's younger brother had promised at breakfast to help her paint the backyard fence. By noon, Ana had finished three sides by herself. It was then that her brother appeared at the gate, holding a brush that was still perfectly dry, and asked brightly whether there was anything left for him to do.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe the tools Ana uses to paint the fence
To show, through a single scene, that Ana's brother did not keep his promise to help her
To explain why Ana prefers to work alone
To show how Ana and her brother settle a long-standing disagreement
explanation:
Stories make their point through what happens, so look at how the details fit together.

The brother promises to help. By noon Ana has done three sides alone. He finally shows up with a brush that's still perfectly dry and cheerfully asks if anything is left.

That dry brush is the key detail: he never helped at all. The scene exists to show he broke his promise. That's choice B.

rationales.A: The only tool mentioned is the brother's brush, and it matters because it's dry, not to describe painting tools.
rationales.C: Ana worked alone because her brother didn't show up, not because she likes working alone.
rationales.D: There's no long running disagreement and no resolution in the scene.

passage: Many city planners favor planting trees along streets because trees provide shade and lower summer temperatures. Some residents, however, object that tree roots can crack sidewalks and that falling leaves clog storm drains. Planners in one city have tried to address these concerns by choosing tree species with deep roots and by scheduling extra street cleaning each autumn.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents objections that the final sentence describes efforts to address.
It provides evidence supporting the planners' preference for street trees.
It states the main argument that the rest of the text defends.
It explains in greater detail the benefits of trees mentioned in the first sentence.
explanation:
Track how the sentences talk to each other.

Sentence 1: planners like street trees for shade. Sentence 2, with "however": residents complain about cracked sidewalks and clogged drains. Sentence 3: planners respond with deep rooted trees (for the sidewalks) and extra cleaning (for the leaves).

So the second sentence raises the problems that the last sentence answers. That's choice A.

rationales.B: The second sentence raises problems with street trees, so it works against the planners' view, not for it.
rationales.C: The text doesn't defend the complaints. It shows how planners responded to them.
rationales.D: The second sentence is about drawbacks, not benefits.

passage: For many years, scientists believed that a certain species of frog had vanished from the mountain streams where it once lived. Then a team of researchers revisiting the area heard an unfamiliar call one night and, after hours of searching, found a small population of the frogs. The researchers now think the frogs survived by retreating to cooler, higher streams that earlier surveys had never explored.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a research method and then evaluates its strengths and weaknesses.
It presents a hypothesis about why frogs disappear and then confirms it with new data.
It describes a long-held belief, presents a discovery that overturned it, and offers an explanation for that discovery.
It compares two frog species and explains why only one of them survived.
explanation:
Label each sentence's job.

Sentence 1: scientists believed the frog had vanished. Sentence 2: researchers found some. Sentence 3: they suggest how the frogs survived.

Old belief, a discovery that overturned it, and an explanation. That's choice C.

rationales.A: The search is mentioned briefly, but no method is weighed for strengths and weaknesses.
rationales.B: The discovery shows the frogs didn't disappear, so nothing about why frogs disappear is confirmed.
rationales.D: Only one kind of frog is discussed.

passage: In an essay, a historian of science notes that the telescope is often credited with transforming astronomy almost overnight. She points out, though, that early telescopes produced blurry images and that many astronomers continued to rely on careful naked-eye observation for decades. The telescope's influence, she argues, was real but gradual, growing steadily as lens-making improved.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that the telescope had little lasting effect on astronomy
To explain how techniques for making lenses improved over time
To describe the methods astronomers used for naked-eye observation
To present a historian's view that qualifies a common belief about the telescope's effect on astronomy
explanation:
The text starts with what people often say: the telescope changed astronomy almost overnight. The historian doesn't reject that completely. She agrees the effect was real but says it was gradual, because early telescopes were blurry and old methods lasted for decades.

Adjusting a belief without throwing it out is called qualifying it. That's choice D.

On hard purpose questions, notice whether the writer flatly rejects an idea or just refines it.

rationales.A: She calls the telescope's influence "real." She only questions how fast it came, so "little lasting effect" goes too far.
rationales.B: Better lenses are mentioned only as the reason the influence grew. They aren't the focus.
rationales.C: Naked eye observation is mentioned as evidence for her point, but its methods are never described.

passage:
The following text is from a story.

Mira had rehearsed the speech for weeks. She knew every pause, every gesture, every place where the audience was supposed to laugh. But when she stepped to the microphone and saw her grandfather in the front row, wearing the same gray suit he had worn to her mother's graduation, the words she had memorized seemed suddenly to belong to someone else.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the first two sentences in the text as a whole?
choices: They reveal that Mira has already delivered the speech to many audiences.
They establish how thoroughly Mira has prepared, which sets up a contrast with her reaction in the final sentence.
They explain why Mira's grandfather has come to hear her speak.
They describe how the audience responds to Mira's speech.
explanation:
The first two sentences pile up how prepared Mira is: weeks of practice, every pause, every gesture. Then "But" turns everything around. When she sees her grandfather, the words she memorized suddenly feel like someone else's.

The opening builds up her preparation so the ending can contrast with it. That's choice B.

When a story spends lines on one feeling and then says "But," the opening is usually there to set up a contrast.

rationales.A: She "rehearsed" the speech. Nothing says she has given it to audiences before.
rationales.C: The grandfather appears only in the last sentence, and no reason for his visit is given.
rationales.D: "Supposed to laugh" describes what she planned for in rehearsal, not how a real audience reacted.

passage: Linguists have observed that when two communities that speak different languages trade regularly, they sometimes develop a simplified shared language in order to communicate. Such languages typically have small vocabularies and few grammatical rules. Yet when children grow up speaking one of these languages as their first language, it often becomes far more complex within a generation, gaining many new words and grammatical structures.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a development that contrasts with the simplicity described in the previous sentence.
It provides an example of the limited grammar described in the previous sentence.
It explains why communities that trade regularly develop shared languages.
It challenges the linguists' observation presented in the first sentence.
explanation:
Look at the word "Yet" at the start of the last sentence. It signals a turn.

The second sentence says these shared languages are simple, with few words and few rules. The last sentence says that once children grow up speaking them, they quickly become much more complex.

So the last sentence describes a change that contrasts with the simplicity just described. That's choice A.

rationales.B: The last sentence is about the language becoming richer, not an example of its limited grammar.
rationales.C: Why communities form these languages (to communicate) appears in the first sentence.
rationales.D: The last sentence adds what happens next. It doesn't question that these languages form.
